### 1.1 I143 scope retained

The annular K0 is non-effective. Secondary doubling uses the unweighted gauge, away from the pole, with distance to the artificial spheres; physical zero boundary remains. Bounded RHS gives boundary W^(2,r) on the common one-sided C^(1,1) charts, and Hölder coefficients freeze without differentiation. Coupling and the strong minimum principle recover both positive limit components from joint nonvanishing. The amplitude equations have determinant 1-pq. This is not circular use of H143.

H143 includes possibly unbounded solutions continuous at the boundary origin. All-radius annular decay and sigma=alpha+beta+2-n>0 give integrable cross energies and absolute gradient product at infinity. Local origin continuity, A,B>=0, and zero trace give bounded local RHS and gradients. Cross multiplication gives F=I=G. On the plane, the dilation boundary term vanishes because x·nu=0, not because normal derivatives vanish. The sphere terms are O(R^-sigma), and gamma_w F=0 contradicts positivity. Singular origin profiles are outside this scope.

The concentration scale lambda, pole distance |x0|, and physical boundary distance remain distinct. The annular bound controls |x0|/lambda; a normalized component and a gradient envelope give a positive boundary distance. Weights do not freeze at the boundary pole. In F143 the coefficient errors are additive RHS errors, with radial integral `1+int_1^(2R) t^(theta-sigma-1)dt`; curvature uses `1+int_1^(2R)t^-sigma dt`. Both logarithmic cases are retained. Eliminating I and F-G gives gamma_w(F+G)/2. The normalization ball in N143 uses one positive component and its distance from the pole. R is chosen before lambda, with K0 still an explicit non-effective dependency. Full-domain uniformity needs the global atlas, collar and diameter data, not a pole chart alone.

I146's numerical representation is appropriately restricted to computable real names plus certified rational positive margins and numerical geometry/modulus envelopes. Arbitrary real symbols are not algorithms. No unnamed elliptic constant is allowed to conceal K0. ### 1.2 A146 constants, positive masses and signed remainder

With `d_n=k_n(2^(2-n)-3^(2-n))`, the B_(4r) Green lower bound on B_r×B_r is valid: the Newton singularity is at least k_n(2r)^(2-n), while the harmonic boundary correction is at most k_n(3r)^(2-n). For f=bU^q and g=aV^p,

`M_f >= A_f r^[n+(2-n)q] M_g^q`,
`M_g >= A_g r^[n+(2-n)p] M_f^p`.

Both masses are positive. Combining and dividing gives exactly

`C_f=(A_f A_g^q)^[-1/(pq-1)]`,
`C_g=(A_g A_f^p)^[-1/(pq-1)]`,

and powers n-2-beta0 and n-2-alpha0. Hölder gives n-alpha0 for U and n-beta0 for V because q alpha0=beta0+2 and p beta0=alpha0+2. The equality case 4r=L uses increasing inner radii, not an assumed trace on the outer sphere.

For s=L/8 the remainder is **h=H-J**, not a nonnegative harmonic function. H is the nonnegative harmonic extension of the actual sphere values, bounded by U; J is the positive ball correction. Mean-value bounds on s/8 balls give the stated 8^n L1 factor. The correction denominator is at least 1/4 for |x|<=s/2, |y|<=s. Its value and derivative bounds are respectively k_n 2^(n-2)s^(2-n) and k_n(n-2)2^(n-1)s^(1-n): the derivative estimate uses the norm of the affine vector in the quadratic denominator, rather than bounding its coordinates separately. Interior harmonic differentiation and these bounds fit the deliberately enlarged original D_U,D_V. Actual sphere data remain in H.

A146.4 is the mass of f on B2 times sup|h_U|. A146.5 is that mass times sup|grad h_U| and ||X||; its signed additional term is retained. A146.6 follows from the mean-value difference over a length at most 2 delta d(x), followed by integration of the level from 0 to f(x). The factor is ||d h_e||_infinity, not a missing extra level integral. The dyadic far-potential powers use the outer annulus radius; the source's truncated-potential bound excludes the near singularity at distance ell. All radii used are <=2s, so A146.1 is available. ### 1.3 Hölder retention and freezing

For 0<theta<=1, delta<=theta/8 implies `(1-delta)^(1/theta)>=1/2`; for example log(1-delta)>=-delta/(1-delta)>=-theta/7. If an interval containing x has length <=ell=delta d(x)^m, then inf_I d>=(1-delta)d(x), and m>=1/theta+1 ensures the interval passes `|I|<=2delta(inf_I d)^(1/theta)`. The coefficient endpoint error is C H delta^theta d(x)U. Multiplication by w is controlled using dw<=C eta. With k=n(m+1), N=k+n+2 the low-level exponent is N-1-k=n+1; the two far-localization powers are 2m+2n+1 and m+2n+2. The cap power N-n-1+m is >=N because m>=n+3. These are all positive. ### 1.4 B146 and C146

Writing a=x_n,b=y_n,Q_t=|x-y|²+4tab, differentiation of the Newton difference gives exactly

`G=(2ab/S_n) int_0^1 Q_t^(-n/2)dt`.

For a tangent L-Lipschitz vector field, `S=X_n(x)/a+X_n(y)/b` obeys |S|<=2L and `|D_X Q_t|<=2L Q_t`. The positive integrand therefore has logarithmic derivative bounded by (n+2)L. This proves B146.2 with the original constant. For X=x the derivative is exactly (2-n)G. A fixed O(E) bound is not an arbitrarily small pressure loss.

For the C146 test, put u=|y|²/(4r²). Direct differentiation gives

`Delta[y_n(1-u)^3]=(3 y_n/(2r²))(1-u)[-(n+2)+(n+6)u]`.

On 0<=u<=1 its absolute value is at most (3/2)(n+6)y_n/r². The test and its first derivative vanish on the artificial sphere; both U and the test vanish on the plane. Thus both Green boundary terms vanish. On B_r the factor is at least 27/64. Direct integration fits the original oversized M_n.

The reflected ball correction has positive sign: Q(x,Ry)=Q(x,y)+4x_n y_n/s², while the exponent (2-n)/2 is negative. Its difference has an x_n y_n factor. For its gradient, differentiate the integral of the first normal derivative of the ball correction in y; the relevant second derivatives have denominators >=1/4 and are bounded by a constant smaller than the original E_n. Thus the original E_n and B_n=4n+E_n M_n suffice. Odd reflection is used only for H_s, the bounded harmonic extension. The signed remainder H_s-J_s has |h|<=B_n x_n/s and |grad h|<=B_n/s.

The tail uses kernel decay |y|^-n multiplied by the first-moment growth r^(n-1). Each dyadic term is proportional to 2^-j/R. Its outer radii are <=2s; s<L/4 ensures the moment test fits. Summation gives the original 2^n C_n M_n factors. At the plane the normal derivative is `2y_n/[S_n(|x'-y'|²+y_n²)^(n/2)]`, positive and generally nonzero.

The thin-plane bound integrates y_n^p up to tau and is an additive bound at fixed R under a known Q_R. Rescaling changes that envelope and the normalization. It does not establish epsilon E+C_epsilon uniformly in the dilation class. The non-tangential image term depends on both s-t and s+t; the original parallel-line trapezoid cannot be reused unchanged. ### C219: one-site coupled spectral deformation

Fix d>=3, a compact band strictly within the ordinary-adjacency clean edges, and a fixed 0<w<w0(d,band) with iid uniform potentials in [-w,w]. Let G_n be uniform among simple labelled d-regular graphs, n>d, nd even, with no further conditioning. Fix E in the band, rho=rho_(d,w)(E), a uniform independent vertex v, and s in a fixed compact real interval. Consider the path of locally finite measures

`Xi_n(s)=sum_i delta_[n rho(lambda_i(H_n+s e_v e_v^T)-E)]`.

Candidate: convergence in C of s, with the vague topology on locally finite counting measures, to the interlacing deformation determined by zeros of 1+s M(z), with the poles at s=0. The proposed Weyl function is

`M(z)=Re m_o(E+i0)+(Im m_o(E+i0)/pi) PV sum_i Z_i²/(xi_i-z)`,

where xi is unit-intensity GOE bulk, Z_i are independent real standard Gaussians, and the random tree environment has its original iid uniform potentials. Independence and the symmetric principal-value convention are part of the target, not consequences of eigenvalue convergence alone. Degenerate finite eigenvalues have probability zero: the discriminant is a nonzero polynomial in the continuously distributed diagonal entries. For a simple eigenvalue, the derivative is |u_i(v)|² with ||u_i||=1; the unfolded derivative is n rho |u_i(v)|². A formal derivative cannot bypass uniformity in s or identification of the real Weyl constant.

**Screen:** the actual weak-disorder introduction already says that the proof identifies conditional Gaussian marks with variance Im m_o/(pi rho), and constructs sampled Weyl functions and exact rank-one changes. Therefore a bare Gaussian-mark theorem is not a fresh target. ## 3. C224 route A: exact resampling histories, not monotone thresholds

The complete source Sections 5, 6 and 7 were read through their proof endings. Section 5 defines kernels for **arbitrary centered signed weights on the entire finite history space**, not just increasing histories. Its forest proof uses necessary local influence and fair constant histories outside insertions. It gives the summable majorant `C^k k^[-(1-g/2)k] product ||w_i||_TV`, g<2, and O(q_e) for terms where two replicas select the same site. Section 6's necklace map is constant or identity at a single bit; it acts coordinatewise on any inserted history. Its pointwise signed factorization therefore also applies to histories with a 1-to-0 change. The annular exchange, protection of the second replica, ordering of its cutoffs, and relative errors remain precisely those in the stipulated operation. Section 7 calibrates q_e=1/E N_e(Q0) and proves r_e/q_e ->1/B with common B>0.

## 4. C224 route B: an actual temporal estimate in the target model

### 4.1 Reversible-clock lemma

Fix any finite geometry and any finite vector F of Boolean observables of its fair independent bits. Monotonicity is unnecessary. Let `I_v(omega)=1{F(omega^v)!=F(omega)}`, `N_F=sum_v I_v`, and let J_F[0,h] count times the vector changes. Refresh every bit at rate r. The flip generator is

`L f=(r/2)sum_v [f(omega^v)-f(omega)]`.

It is reversible for fair product measure pi. Crucially I_v(omega^v)=I_v(omega). If P_t is its semigroup and lambda=(r/2)N_F, then stationarity and the Markov property give exactly

`E_pi J_F[0,h] = h E_pi lambda`,

`E_pi[J_F[0,h](J_F[0,h]-1)] = 2 int_0^h (h-t) <lambda,P_t lambda>_pi dt`.  (D149.1)

Proof of the second identity: for the first counted transition, sum `(r/2) I_v(omega) (P_t lambda)(omega^v)` against pi. Change omega to omega^v separately in each summand. Invariance of pi and I_v turns the sum into `<lambda,P_t lambda>`. Integrate ordered pairs of jump times and multiply by two. The L2 contraction of P_t gives

`P_pi(J_F[0,h]>=2) <= r² h² E_pi N_F² /8`.  (D149.2)

This is an estimate for the actual reversible independent-resampling dynamics conditional on its actual geometry. ## 5. A paid quantitative spectral-transform partial

For C234, write H_mu(z)=int(z-lambda)^-1 mu(dlambda), z>e_mu. The source's convention sets b_mu(x) to the root H_mu(b)=x when it exists, otherwise to e_mu, and R_mu(x)=b_mu(x)-1/x. Its bounds give b_mu(x)<=e_mu+1/x and |R_mu|<=K.

For `0<x<=1/(4K)`, both roots are uncapped and lie in `[1/x-K,1/x+K]`. At a root, the reciprocal integrand is 4x²-Lipschitz in lambda. On the segment between the two roots, `-H'_mu >= 4x²/9`. Kantorovich's elementary coupling bound and inversion therefore give `|R_mu(x)-R_nu(x)|<=9 epsilon`. At x=0 the difference of means is at most epsilon.

For `1/(4K)<=x<=1`, let t>0 and put `a=max(b_mu(x),e_nu)+t`. Then a is at least t above both supports and a-b_mu<=delta+t. Also H_mu(a)<=x, including the capped case, so `H_nu(a)<=x+epsilon/t²`. If b_nu<=a there is nothing further to prove. Otherwise b_nu is uncapped, a<b_nu<=5K, and on [a,b_nu], `-H'_nu>=1/(36K²)`. Consequently

`b_nu-b_mu <= delta+t+36K² epsilon/t²`.

Interchange mu and nu. Choosing `t=(72K² epsilon)^(1/3)` gives the asserted bound with 7 (the exact coefficient `(3/2)72^(1/3)` is smaller). If epsilon=0 the measures agree and no division is used. Hence

`||R_mu-R_nu||_[0,1] <= max{9epsilon,delta+7K^(2/3)epsilon^(1/3)}`.  (S149)

The source's actual variational operation adds the common S(p), evaluates R at D_p(r) in [0,1], then takes the infimum. It gives exactly the factor 1/2 in C234, with no exchange of infimum and supremum. This bound includes the edge-capped branch and needs no derivative of the limiting pressure.
